title: The Czech Alphabet: How Every Letter Sounds
description: Say the whole Czech alphabet — every vowel and consonant, from a to ž — with its exact sound and an example word. This is the foundation everything else builds on.

data.question_en: Compared to English, how do Czech letters sound?
options: Letters change sound depending on the word, like English
Each letter has one consistent sound, almost always
Vowels are silent at the end of words
The sound depends on where the stress falls
data.explanation: Czech is (almost) perfectly phonetic: each letter maps to one sound, so once you know the letters you can read any word aloud. Stress is always on the FIRST syllable and never changes a letter's sound.

exercises.prompt: The five short vowels: a e i o u

data.question_en: The short vowels a, e, i, o, u sound roughly like which English words?
options: cup, bed, sit, for, put — a-e-i-o-u
data.explanation: a=matka (mother), e=pes (dog), i=pivo (beer), o=okno (window), u=ruka (hand). Keep them short and crisp. The letter y is pronounced exactly like i — byt (flat) sounds like 'bit'.

exercises.prompt: Long vowels: á é í ó ú ů ý

data.question_en: What does the čárka (á) or kroužek (ů) mark do?
options: Holds the vowel about twice as long
data.explanation: The čárka (´) and kroužek (˚) make a vowel LONG — held about twice as long: káva (á), mléko (é), víno (í), dům (ů), sýr (ý). ú and ů are both a long 'oo': ú starts a word (úkol), ů comes later (dům). Length can change meaning — byt (flat) vs být (to be).

exercises.prompt: Say it aloud — short vs long a

data.question_en: What does ě do to the consonant before it?
options: Nothing — it is just a short e
Softens it: dě, tě, ně sound like 'dye, tye, nye'; mě sounds like 'mnye'
data.explanation: ě never stands alone — it softens the consonant in front of it. děti (children) = 'dye-ti', město (city) = 'mnye-sto', měsíc (month). You'll meet ě constantly.

exercises.prompt: Match each háček consonant to its English sound
exercises.answer_key: č=ch as in 'church', š=sh as in 'ship', ž=s as in 'measure', ř=unique Czech sound (rolled r + ž)

data.question_en: How is c pronounced in Czech (cukr, noc)?
data.explanation: c is ALWAYS 'ts', never 'k' or 's'. cukr (sugar) = 'tsukr', noc (night) = 'nots', práce (work). This trips up English speakers the most.

options: two separate letters, c then h
one single letter, like 'ch' in Scottish 'loch' / German 'Bach'
data.explanation: ch is ONE letter (a raspy sound made in the back of the throat): chléb (bread), chci (I want), ucho (ear). In the dictionary it comes after h, not under c.

exercises.prompt: Three consonants that look familiar but aren't: h, j, r

options: j sounds like 'y' in 'yes'; h is a soft voiced 'h'; r is rolled/trilled
h is always silent; r is like English r
j and r are both silent before a vowel
data.explanation: j = 'y': jablko (apple), juice→džus. h is voiced and breathy: hora (mountain). r is rolled with the tip of the tongue: ryba (fish), ráno (morning). None of them sound like their English look-alikes.

exercises.prompt: Say the most famous Czech sound: ř

data.question_en: How are ď, ť, ň (and d, t, n before i or ě) pronounced?
options: Softened — like 'd' in British 'duty', 't' in 'tune', 'ñ' in 'canyon'
data.explanation: The háček (or a following i/ě) softens them: kůň (horse) ends in a soft ň, chuť (taste) ends in soft ť, loď (boat) ends in soft ď. Also děti, tělo, není — the d/t/n there are soft.

exercises.prompt: Listen and type — the letter ž

data.note: ž sounds like the 's' in 'measure'. žena = woman. First-syllable stress: ŽE-na.

exercises.prompt: Listen and type — long ý and the letter s

data.note: s is always a plain 's' (never 'z'); ý is a long 'ee'. sýr = cheese, said 'seer'.

data.question_en: Which letters appear almost only in words borrowed from other languages?
data.explanation: Native Czech spells these sounds differently, so q, w, x are rare and mostly in loanwords (taxi, watt). ó is also mostly foreign (móda = fashion). Everything else you've met is fully native.
